summary: 1 Thessalonians is probably Paul's oldest surviving letter and, for that reason, one of the first Christian writings. Paul, Silvanus and Timothy had been forced to leave Thessalonica shortly after founding there a church made up mainly of people who had turned away from idols (1:9). On receiving from Timothy good news about their steadfastness, Paul writes with relief, recalls the time he spent in the city and reinforces the teaching they received about holy living and work. He also answers a question that was grieving them: what happens to the brothers who die before the coming of the Lord (4:13–18).
name: The title Pros Thessalonikeis A, “First to the Thessalonians,” comes from the greeting “to the church of the Thessalonians” (1:1); the number distinguishes it from the second letter to the same church. The city was named after Thessalonike, sister of Alexander the Great and wife of Cassander, who founded it around 316 BC.
facts: 13th book of the New Testament; 8th of Paul's letters, in canonical order

structure.title: Gratitude for the church
structure.text: The faith, love and hope of the Thessalonians have become known in Macedonia and Achaia.

structure.title: Memories of the mission
structure.text: Paul recalls how he worked with his own hands so as not to be a burden to anyone, the church's suffering, the forced separation, the sending of Timothy from Athens and the joy at the news he brought.

structure.title: Instructions
structure.text: Holiness in the body, brotherly love and work; hope regarding those who have died; the day of the Lord, which will come by surprise; and a series of brief counsels for the life of the church.

extra.title: Paul's oldest letter
extra.text: If the most common dating is right, this letter was written some twenty years after the death of Jesus, before any gospel. In it already appear faith, love and hope together (1:3; 5:8), the expectation of the Lord's coming and the order that the letter “be read to all the brothers” (5:27), a sign that letters were read aloud at the gatherings.

people.name: Paul
people.note: founder of the church; tried more than once to return, but was hindered (2:17–18)

people.name: Silvanus
people.note: co-author of the greeting; he is the Silas of Acts, Paul's companion on the second journey

people.name: Timothy
people.note: sent from Athens to strengthen the church, returns with good news (3:1–6)

writing.tradition: Paul's authorship was accepted without dispute in the early Church. Since Timothy rejoined Paul after the stay in Athens, the letter was placed in Corinth, during the year and a half Paul spent there (Acts 18:5, 11).
writing.academic: 1 Thessalonians is among the seven letters that practically all scholars attribute to Paul, alongside Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians and Philemon, and is generally dated c. 50–51, in Corinth. Paul's stay in that city is dated with relative certainty by an inscription at Delphi that mentions the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:12). A debated point is 2:14–16, which speaks harshly of the Jews who killed the Lord and persecuted the prophets: some scholars consider it a later addition, perhaps after the destruction of Jerusalem in 70, but most keep it as part of the letter, read in the context of local conflicts. It is also debated whether the letter is a single one or the combination of two, a minority hypothesis.

events.intro: The founding of the church and the letter fit into a few months of Paul's second journey, according to the itinerary of Acts 17–18. The dates are approximate.

context: Thessalonica (today's Thessaloniki, in Greece) was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a port on the Thermaic Gulf crossed by the Via Egnatia. It was a free city, with its own magistrates (the “politarchs” of Acts 17:6, a title confirmed by inscriptions) and had temples of various gods, a local cult of Cabirus and honors paid to Rome and the emperors. According to Acts, Paul preached in the synagogue for three Sabbaths and won over some Jews and many devout Greeks, but opposition led to a riot and his departure by night. The letter indicates that the converts continued to suffer hostility from their own countrymen (2:14).
